examples.en: Dark clouds are gathering, so it looks like rain is coming soon.

examples.ko: 아이가 눈을 비비는 걸 보니 곧 잠이 들려나 봐요.
examples.en: The child is rubbing their eyes, so it looks like they will fall asleep soon.

examples.ko: 승규가 부엌에서 냄비를 꺼내는 걸 보니 라면을 끓이려나 봐요.
examples.en: Seunggyu is taking a pot out in the kitchen, so it looks like they will cook ramen.

examples.ko: 저쪽에서 사람들이 모이는 걸 보니 곧 행사가 시작되려나 보다.
examples.en: People are gathering over there, so it looks like the event is about to begin.

compare.difference: “-나 보다” guesses at what is the case now or was; “-으려나 보다” guesses at what is about to happen.

pair.en: It seems to be raining.
It seems it is going to rain.

compare.difference: “-으려나?” is a question to oneself (“I wonder if…”); “-으려나 보다” is a guess from evidence.

pair.en: I wonder if it will rain.
It looks like it will rain.

pitfalls.note: It needs a sign the speaker has seen, and it is about someone or something else, not the speaker's plans.
pitfalls.right: 민준이가 가방을 싸는 걸 보니 내일 떠나려나 보다.
pitfalls.en: Minjun is packing a bag, so it looks like they will leave tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the ending is “-려나”.
pitfalls.en: It looks like it will rain soon.

label: with, over; using something
meaning_en: An expression with two uses: a tool, a means or a material (“with, using X”), and the object or occasion of an action, often a quarrel (“over, about X”).
usage: It attaches to nouns as “을 가지고” after a final consonant and “를 가지고” after a vowel. In the first sense it is followed by a verb of making or doing (“만들다”, “고치다”). In the second it is followed by a verb of reacting (“화내다”, “싸우다”, “비난하다”), and the noun is typically a small matter. It is a different thing from the verb phrase “가지고 가다/오다” (“take, bring”).

examples.ko: 승규는 폐휴지를 가지고 멋진 장식품을 만들어 냈다.
examples.en: Seunggyu made a fine ornament out of waste paper.

examples.ko: 우리 집은 직접 키운 포도를 가지고 와인을 만들었다.
examples.en: My family made wine with grapes we grew ourselves.

examples.ko: 저는 이 작은 도구 하나를 가지고 모든 수리를 합니다.
examples.en: I do all the repairs with this one small tool.

examples.ko: 별것 아닌 일을 가지고 싸우지 말자.
examples.en: Let's not fight over something trivial.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 사소한 실수를 가지고 계속 나를 비난했다.
examples.en: That person kept criticizing me over a minor mistake.

compare.difference: In the sense of a tool the two are close in meaning; “(으)로” is shorter and “를 가지고” stresses the thing in hand.

pair.en: I made a chair with wood.
I made a chair out of wood.

compare.difference: “를 가지고” names the thing quarreled over; “때문에” names the cause.

pair.en: We fought over a small matter.
We fought because of a small matter.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “를”, not “을”.
pitfalls.en: I made wine with grapes.

label: maybe if, but otherwise not
meaning_en: An expression meaning “if X were so, it might be a different story, but as things are…”: it grants that the main point would hold only under the stated condition, and says it does not hold in the actual case.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-으면 몰라도”, or “-면 몰라도” after a vowel or ㄹ, and to a noun as “이면 몰라도” or “(이)라면 몰라도”. The condition is the exceptional case, and the main clause denies or rejects the usual case (often with “-는데”, “-면 안 되다”, “-기 힘들다”). It is conversational.

examples.ko: 차가 멈추어 있으면 몰라도 운전 중에는 통화하시면 안 돼요.
examples.en: It might be fine if the car were stopped, but you must not take calls while driving.

examples.ko: 가족이 많으면 몰라도 부부 단둘이서 사는데 이 집은 너무 넓다.
examples.en: It might do for a large family, but for a couple living alone this house is too big.

examples.ko: 초보면 몰라도 경력 십 년의 전문가가 그런 실수를 하다니 이해가 안 돼요.
examples.en: A beginner might, but I can't understand an expert with ten years' experience making that mistake.

examples.ko: 어린아이면 몰라도 다 큰 어른이 그렇게 떼를 쓰면 안 되지.
examples.en: A small child maybe, but a grown adult shouldn't throw a tantrum like that.

examples.ko: 돈이 많으면 몰라도 우리 형편에 그렇게 비싼 차는 무리야.
examples.en: If we had lots of money, maybe, but a car that expensive is out of reach for our means.

compare.difference: “-더라도” says that something holds even under a condition; “-으면 몰라도” says it might hold only under that condition.

pair.en: If we had lots of money, maybe, but it is too much for us.
Even if we had lots of money, that is too much.

compare.difference: “-을지 몰라도” means “it may be so, but…”; “-으면 몰라도” means “only if it were so”.

pair.en: They may be rich, but they are stingy.
For a rich person maybe, but this much is too much.

pitfalls.note: After a noun that ends in a consonant the “이” of “이다” is needed.
pitfalls.wrong: 학생면 몰라도 어른이 그러면 안 된다.
pitfalls.right: 학생이면 몰라도 어른이 그러면 안 된다.
pitfalls.en: A student maybe, but an adult shouldn't do that.

label: despite, in spite of
meaning_en: A formal expression meaning “despite, in spite of X”: what follows is different from, or the opposite of, what X would lead one to expect.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “에도 불구하고”, and often to nouns that name a condition, an effort or an obstacle (“날씨”, “노력”, “반대”). The clause after it states the unexpected outcome. For a clause use “-는데도 불구하고”, and for a noun made with “이다” use “임에도 불구하고”. It is formal and common in news and essays.

examples.ko: 추운 날씨에도 불구하고 공원은 나들이객으로 붐볐다.
examples.en: Despite the cold weather, the park was crowded with people out for a stroll.

examples.ko: 선수의 뛰어난 활약에도 불구하고 팀은 패배하고 말았다.
examples.en: Despite the player's outstanding performance, the team ended up losing.

examples.ko: 여러 번의 실패에도 불구하고 지수는 포기하지 않았다.
examples.en: Despite repeated failures, Jisu did not give up.

examples.ko: 부모님의 만류에도 불구하고 나는 유학을 떠나기로 했다.
examples.en: Despite my parents' attempts to stop me, I decided to go abroad to study.

examples.ko: 높은 가격에도 불구하고 그 제품은 불티나게 팔렸다.
examples.en: Despite the high price, the product sold like hot cakes.

compare.difference: “에도 불구하고” follows a noun; “-는데도 불구하고” follows a clause.

pair.en: Despite the cold, I went out.
Although it was cold, I went out.

compare.difference: “에도 불구하고” says the result is the opposite of what X suggests; “에 상관없이” says X does not matter.

pair.en: The event was held despite the weather.
The event is held regardless of the weather.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows must go against what the noun suggests.
pitfalls.wrong: 추운 날씨에도 불구하고 우리는 두꺼운 옷을 입고 나갔다.
pitfalls.right: 추운 날씨에도 불구하고 우리는 가벼운 옷차림으로 나갔다.
pitfalls.en: Despite the cold weather, we went out in light clothes.

topik_tip: In 읽기 passages “에도 불구하고” marks a contrast; the clause that follows goes against what the noun leads you to expect.

label: even though
meaning_en: A connective expression meaning “even though X, still Y”: the main clause happens in spite of the situation in the first clause, which is an actual fact.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는데도”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은데도”, to “이다” as “인데도”, and after “-었-” (“했는데도”). The first clause is something that has really happened or is true, and the main clause is the surprising result. For a hypothetical, use “-아도/어도”.

examples.ko: 조금 전에 밥을 먹었는데도 또 배가 고파요.
examples.en: I ate a little while ago, but I'm hungry again.

examples.ko: 밖에 눈이 많이 오는데도 거리에 사람이 많다.
examples.en: Even though it is snowing hard outside, there are many people on the street.

examples.ko: 열심히 공부했는데도 성적이 오르지 않았다.
examples.en: Even though I studied hard, my grades did not go up.

examples.ko: 몸이 아픈데도 지수는 약속을 지키려고 나왔다.
examples.en: Even though they were sick, Jisu came out to keep the appointment.

examples.ko: 주말인데도 사무실에는 불이 켜져 있었다.
examples.en: Even though it was the weekend, the lights were on in the office.

compare.difference: “-아도/어도” can concede a hypothetical; “-는데도” takes an actual fact.

pair.en: I will go even if it rains.
I went even though it was raining.

compare.difference: “-는데” just gives background and can lead anywhere; “-는데도” says the result goes against it.

pair.en: I studied hard, and my grades went up.
Even though I studied hard, my grades did not go up.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은데도”.
pitfalls.en: Even though I was sick, I came out to keep the appointment.

pitfalls.note: After a noun it is “인데도”.
pitfalls.en: Even though it was the weekend, the lights were on in the office.

label: see it through, manage to
meaning_en: An expression meaning to carry something through to the end by one's own effort, usually despite difficulty: “manage to do, see through, pull off”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-아 내다/-어 내다” (“참아 내다”, “이겨 내다”, “만들어 내다”). The verb is one that needs effort, patience or endurance, and the sense is that the person finally achieves the result. It is not used for easy, routine acts. It is written in the same way in both speech and writing, and “내다” is separate from “-어 버리다”, which marks completion with relief or regret.

examples.ko: 꾸준한 노력은 기적을 만들어 낸다.
examples.en: Steady effort produces miracles.

examples.ko: 아이는 아파도 울지 않고 끝까지 참아 내는 모습이 대견했다.
examples.en: It was admirable how the child held out to the end without crying, even though it hurt.

examples.ko: 지수는 포기하고 싶은 순간들을 이겨 내고 결국 마라톤을 완주했다.
examples.en: Jisu overcame the moments of wanting to give up and finally finished the marathon.

examples.ko: 연구팀은 십 년 만에 새로운 치료법을 찾아냈다.
examples.en: The research team found a new treatment after ten years.

examples.ko: 어려운 환경에서도 끝까지 버텨 내는 사람들이 결국 성공한다.
examples.en: In the end, people who endure to the very end even in a harsh environment succeed.

compare.difference: “-어 버리다” marks something as done and over, often with relief or regret; “-어 내다” marks something achieved through effort.

pair.en: I got all my homework done.
I saw the hard homework through to the end.

compare.difference: “-고 말다” says something ends up happening, often against one's wish; “-어 내다” says the result was won by effort.

pair.en: In the end I won (it ended that way).
In the end I overcame it.

pitfalls.note: The vowel of the stem decides “-아” or “-어”.
pitfalls.en: Even though it hurt, I held out to the end.

pitfalls.note: It suits an act that took effort, not a simple one.
pitfalls.right: 많은 양의 점심을 억지로 다 먹어 냈다.
pitfalls.en: I forced myself to eat all of the huge lunch.

label: since I heard that
meaning_en: An expression for a reason based on what someone said: “since (someone) said that X, I did Y”. It is a contraction of “-는다고 하기에”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다기에/-는다기에”, to adjective stems and past forms as “-다기에” (“바쁘다기에”, “갔다기에”), and to “이다” as “-라기에”. The quoted fact is the basis for what the speaker or someone else then did, and the main clause is normally in the past. It cannot be followed by a command or a suggestion. It is conversational.

examples.ko: 승규가 요즘 스트레스를 많이 받는다기에 같이 노래방에 갔다.
examples.en: Seunggyu said they were under a lot of stress lately, so we went to a karaoke room together.

examples.ko: 조카가 고기를 잘 먹는다기에 불고기를 구워 줬다.
examples.en: My niece or nephew said they liked meat, so I grilled bulgogi for them.

examples.ko: 일기예보에서 내일 비가 온다기에 우산을 챙겨 두었다.
examples.en: The forecast said it would rain tomorrow, so I set an umbrella aside.

examples.ko: 지수가 요즘 많이 바쁘다기에 연락을 하지 않았다.
examples.en: Jisu said they were very busy lately, so I did not get in touch.

examples.ko: 친구가 내일 시험이라기에 같이 도서관에 갔다.
examples.en: A friend said they had an exam tomorrow, so I went to the library together with them.

compare.difference: “-는다고 해서” is the full form; “-는다기에” is its contraction, and the two mean the same.

pair.en: I was told it would rain, so I took an umbrella.
I was told it would rain, so I took an umbrella.

compare.difference: “-는다기에” rests on what the speaker heard; “-길래” rests on what the speaker saw.

pair.en: I was told it would rain, so I took an umbrella.
It was raining, so I took an umbrella.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows reports an action; it cannot be a command.
pitfalls.en: I was told it would rain, so I took an umbrella.

pitfalls.note: After a noun it is “-이라기에”, not “-이다기에”.
pitfalls.en: I was told the exam is tomorrow, so we studied together.

label: meant to, but ended up
meaning_en: An expression for a slip: “I meant to do X, but (instead) did Y”. What is said to have been intended is followed by a different result.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다는/는다는 것이”, and the colloquial contraction is “-ㄴ다는 게”. The following clause states what actually happened, often with “그만” or “-고 말다”, and the result is mismatched with the intention. The subject is typically the speaker. It is used in conversation. It is not used when intention and result agree.

examples.ko: 국수를 삶는다는 것이 라면을 끓였어요.
examples.en: I meant to boil noodles, but I made ramen.

examples.ko: 소금을 넣는다는 것이 설탕을 넣고 말았다.
examples.en: I meant to add salt, but I added sugar.

examples.ko: 물을 마신다는 게 그만 컵을 떨어뜨리고 말았다.
examples.en: I meant to drink some water, but I dropped the cup.

examples.ko: 지수에게 보낸다는 것이 잘못해서 민준이에게 메시지를 보냈다.
examples.en: I meant to send the message to Jisu, but by mistake I sent it to Minjun.

examples.ko: 버스를 탄다는 것이 지하철 입구로 들어와 버렸다.
examples.en: I meant to take the bus, but I walked in at the subway entrance.

compare.difference: “-으려다가” says one was about to do something and did another; “-는다는 것이” says the act itself was mistaken.

pair.en: I was about to add salt, but I added sugar.
I meant to add salt, but I added sugar.

compare.difference: “-으려고 했는데” simply states the plan before a different outcome; “-는다는 것이” makes the mix-up itself the point.

pair.en: I meant to call, but forgot.
I meant to call, but it slipped my mind.

pitfalls.note: The result has to differ from the intention, so the same act cannot follow.
pitfalls.right: 숙제를 한다는 것이 게임을 하고 말았다.
pitfalls.en: I meant to do my homework, but I ended up playing a game.

label: even though, despite the fact
meaning_en: A formal expression meaning “even though, despite the fact that X”: it states a fact and then something that goes against what the fact would lead one to expect.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는데도 불구하고”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은데도 불구하고”, to “이다” as “인데도 불구하고”, and after “-었-”. It is the clause form of “에도 불구하고”. It carries the same meaning as the shorter “-는데도” and sounds more formal. It is common in news and essays.

examples.ko: 지수는 아침부터 서둘렀는데도 불구하고 학교에 늦고 말았다.
examples.en: Even though Jisu hurried from the morning, they ended up late for school.

examples.ko: 소나기가 쏟아지는데도 불구하고 공연장에는 많은 관중이 모였다.
examples.en: Despite the downpour, a large crowd gathered at the concert hall.

examples.ko: 여러 번 실패했는데도 불구하고 포기하지 않았다.
examples.en: Even though I failed many times, I did not give up.

examples.ko: 주말인데도 불구하고 많은 직원이 출근했다.
examples.en: Even though it was the weekend, many employees came to work.

examples.ko: 충분히 설명했는데도 불구하고 학생들은 이해하지 못했다.
examples.en: Even though I explained it thoroughly, the students did not understand.

compare.difference: “-는데도 불구하고” follows a clause; “에도 불구하고” follows a noun.

pair.en: Although it was cold, I went out.
Despite the cold, I went out.

compare.difference: “-지만” is the plain “but”; “-는데도 불구하고” stresses that the result is unexpected.

pair.en: I hurried but was late.
Despite having hurried, I was late.

pitfalls.note: The “도” of “-는데도” cannot be left out.
pitfalls.en: Despite having hurried, I was late for school.

pitfalls.note: After a noun it is “인데도 불구하고”.
pitfalls.en: Even though it was the weekend, I went to work.
